title: The Inventory of Small Things
text:
My grandmother kept a tin of buttons that she had salvaged from every garment she ever discarded. As a child I assumed the tin was merely a container, a bit of domestic clutter, but I came to understand it as a ledger of her life. Each button carried a faint memory: a wedding dress she had unpicked, a coat that had survived three house moves across the country, a school blazer her son had outgrown too quickly. To sift through them was to read an autobiography written in brass and bone.

When she died, the tin passed to me without any note of explanation, and for months it sat unopened on a shelf. Eventually I tipped its contents onto a kitchen table and began arranging the buttons by colour, then by size, then by the stories I half-remembered. The exercise felt less like cataloguing than like eavesdropping on a conversation that had ended before I was old enough to join it. I realised that memoir, like that tin, is rarely about the objects themselves but about the hand that gathered them.

questions.text: According to the first paragraph, what did the grandmother's tin contain?
options: Fabric scraps from her wedding dress

questions.text: According to the second paragraph, how did the narrator first arrange the buttons?
options: By the year they were made
By the name of each owner

questions.text: What does the phrase 'an autobiography written in brass and bone' suggest about the buttons?
options: They reveal the grandmother's life history through the objects she preserved
They were valuable antiques that the family sold after her death
They were handmade by the grandmother as a hobby
They were designed to be used as tools for sewing

questions.text: Why does the narrator describe the act of sorting the buttons as 'eavesdropping'?
options: The narrator was secretly listening to family members talk
The narrator was piecing together a past they had been too young to share in
The buttons made quiet sounds when they were moved
The grandmother had asked the narrator to keep her secrets

paragraph_translations: Büyükannem, attığı her kıyafetten kurtardığı düğmelerle dolu bir teneke saklardı. Çocukken tenekenin sadece bir kap, evin dağınıklığından başka bir şey olmadığını sanırdım; ama zamanla onu hayatının bir kayıt defteri olarak anlamaya başladım. Her düğme soluk bir anıyı taşıyordu: söktüğü bir gelinlik, ülke çapında üç kez ev değiştirmiş ama yine de sağlam kalmış bir palto, oğlunun çok çabuk büyüdüğü için giymediği bir okul ceketi. Bu düğmelerin arasında gezinmek, pirinç ve kemikten yazılmış bir otobiyografiyi okumak gibiydi.

Büyükannem öldüğünde teneke, hiçbir açıklama notu olmadan bana kaldı ve aylarca açılmadan bir rafta durdu. Sonunda içindekileri mutfak masasına döktüm; önce renklerine, sonra boyutlarına, en sonunda da yarım yamalak hatırladığım hikâyelerine göre dizmeye başladım. Bu uğraş bir envanter çıkarmaktan çok, ben büyüyüp katılabilecek yaşa gelmeden biten bir sohbeti dinlemeye benziyordu. Anladım ki anı yazısı, tıpkı o teneke gibi, nesnelerin kendisiyle pek ilgili değildir; asıl konu onları toplayan eldir.
